title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani close

segments.voice: Yesterday: saloks at the close of a reading, and your line: read for the departed. Did you say someone's name, and a line beside it? Today we close a whole stretch: thirty-two days with the ninth Guru. Day six hundred ten.
screen: `SALOKS AT THE CLOSE — READ FOR THE DEPARTED.`

segments.voice: If you had to describe a teacher in four words after a month with them, what would you pick? Not their biography. The feel of them: the voice you'd hear in your head when you needed it. We started this block on the ninth Guru's voice, and its line was calm and plain. Since then we've walked through his shabads in their ragas and all fifty-seven saloks. A wall of sand. Friends in good times. Gold and iron alike. Fear none, frighten none. The days slip by. Rama gone, Ravana gone. Strength gone, strength returned. The Name remains. Today, before we turn to the Ardas, four words for the whole of it. Today: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani, the close.
screen: `FOUR WORDS FOR A TEACHER.` → `A MONTH WITH THE NINTH GURU.` → `BEFORE WE TURN TO THE ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The four words are calm, fearless, detached, and kind. Take them in turn. Calm. His bani has almost no drama in it. Short lines, plain words, the same truths said again and again: it is passing, like a dream, the days slip by. It reads like someone speaking slowly to a friend who is upset. Fearless. The salok we met as fear none, frighten none says, in paraphrase, that the wise one gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one. Sikhs see that line lived out in his death. Tradition remembers that he went to Delhi and gave his life in 1675, and Sikhs honor him as having died for others' freedom to practice their own faith. He's often called Hind di chadar, the shield of India. Detached. The word in his bani is often bairaag, a turning away from clutching, and the picture is gold and iron alike, praise and blame alike. Not cold, but unhooked. It's love without clutching, as one day's line had it. Kind. This one is easy to miss, because his bani talks so much about death. But all that talk of passing is never meant to frighten. It's said the way you'd tell someone you love: we don't have forever, so let's not waste it. Strength gone, then strength returned. All companions gone, then the Name remains. Every hard line turns, sooner or later, toward what stays. That's the ninth Guru's bani: fifty-nine shabads in fifteen ragas, and fifty-seven saloks, most of them two lines long. Small in size. Not small in weight.
screen: `CALM: PLAIN LINES, SAID SLOWLY.` · `FEARLESS: FEAR NONE, FRIGHTEN NONE.` · `DETACHED: GOLD AND IRON ALIKE.` · `KIND: EVERY HARD LINE TURNS.` · then, large: `CALM AND FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry one salok this week. Sit, and let a few of this month's lines pass through your mind: it is passing. Like a dream. Nothing stays. Today or tomorrow. Only you. The Name remains. Nothing equals it. Notice which one catches. Don't choose the wisest; choose the one that tugs. Say it three times, slowly, with your breath. That's the one you'll carry until next week. If you pray, you can follow it with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani close. Calm, fearless, detached, and kind: fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks, small in size, not small in weight.
screen: `GURU TEGH BAHADUR'S BANI CLOSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: calm and fearless. Write the salok you chose somewhere you'll see it, and let it travel with you this week. Tomorrow, the prayer said standing. Day six hundred ten.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in kirtan and his saloks at every bhog, and on the day of his martyrdom, often observed in November or December, gurdwaras sing his bani and tell the story of Delhi.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nirbhau, without fear; a word from the Mool Mantar that Sikhs see lived out in the ninth Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani is all about death.
what it means: it is calm, fearless, detached and kind, and every hard line turns to what stays.
what a scholar hears: 59 shabads across 15 ragas and 57 saloks (Angs 1426–1429); salok 16 (bhai kaahoo ko det nahi) is the classic statement of his fearlessness.
